NO RESCUE
Christmas Eve,
1971.
Somewhere above the Peruvian Amazon.
A seventeen-year-old girl is falling through the sky.
She is still strapped into her seat.
Around her,
there is no airplane anymore.
Only wind,
rain,
and the roar of the air.
Below her,
the treetops spin closer,
green and endless,
like heads of broccoli.
Ninety-two people boarded that flight.
Only one of them would ever walk out of the jungle.
She would do it alone.
Injured.
Half blind.
With a bag of sweets and one sandal.
And the only reason she survived is that,
years before,
her parents had taught her how the jungle thinks.
This is the story of Juliane Koepcke,
and the eleven days nobody came.
This is No Rescue.
True stories of people who survived when no one
was coming.
To understand how a teenage girl walked out of the Amazon,
you have to start with her parents.
Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke was a German zoologist with
an obsession.
South America.
After the war,
he set out for Peru with almost nothing.
He travelled on foot,
and as a stowaway on a ship.
He was detained along the way.
The journey took him about two years.
In 1950,
he finally reached Lima.
Back in Germany,
in the university town of Kiel,
he had met another young scientist.
Maria.
She was an ornithologist,
one of the finest of her generation.
She followed him to Peru,
and together they began to catalogue a continent.
Maria described birds that science had never named before.
Today,
four species carry her name.
Among them,
a hummingbird,
and an owl.
In 1954,
their only child was born in Lima.
Juliane.
Her childhood was not dolls and television.
It was birds,
insects and bones.
And in 1968,
her parents did something most people would call insane.
They moved deep into the rainforest,
to a clearing beside the Yuyapichis River.
They built a research station there,
a house on stilts with a palm roof,
and named it after a local bird.
Panguana.
Juliane was fourteen.
She learned the jungle the way other children
learn a city.
Which plants you never touch.
Which animals only look dangerous.
Which ones really are.
And her father gave her one rule above all others.
If you are ever lost,
find moving water,
and never let it out of your sight.
The stream will take you to a brook.
The brook will take you to a river.
And on the river,
you will find people.
She never imagined she would need it.
By the end of 1971,
Juliane was back in Lima,
finishing school.
Her graduation was on December the twenty-third.
Her mother had wanted to fly out days earlier.
Juliane begged to stay for the ceremony.
Her mother gave in.
The plan was simple.
Fly to Pucallpa on Christmas Eve.
Spend Christmas with her father in the forest.
But by then,
almost every flight was full.
Only one airline still had seats.
LANSA.
Its reputation was terrible.
Sixteen months earlier,
a LANSA plane had crashed in the Andes near Cusco.
Ninety-nine of the hundred people on board were killed.
Hans-Wilhelm had asked his wife never to fly with
that company.
But it was Christmas,
and there were seats,
and it was only an hour's flight.
The aircraft was a Lockheed Electra.
A four-engine turboprop.
It was the last plane the airline had left.
That morning,
the flight was delayed.
Hours went by in the terminal.
Finally,
on December the twenty-fourth,
LANSA Flight 508 took off from Lima.
Ninety-two people on board.
Eighty-six passengers.
Six crew.
Many of them were families,
going home for Christmas,
with wrapped presents in the overhead racks.
Juliane sat by the window,
near the back of the plane.
Her mother sat next to her,
in the middle seat.
Below them,
the Andes.
Then the long eastern slope,
falling into the clouds of the Amazon.
For a while,
it was an ordinary flight.
Then the plane flew into a storm.
Not a small one.
A wall of black cloud,
the kind that builds over the rainforest on
summer afternoons.
The sky went dark in the middle of the day.
The Electra began to shake.
And it did not stop.
For twenty,
maybe thirty minutes,
the pilots kept flying through the turbulence.
Luggage burst out of the overhead compartments.
Presents,
bags and clothes rained down on the passengers.
Through the window,
Juliane saw lightning flashing around the wing.
People were screaming.
Some were praying.
Her mother,
very quietly,
said something Juliane would never forget.
Now it's all over.
Then a blinding light hit the right wing.
Lightning had struck.
An engine burst into flames.
At twelve thirty-six in the afternoon,
about fifteen minutes from Pucallpa,
the right wing tore away.
At roughly three thousand meters,
ten thousand feet,
the Electra broke apart in the air.
One moment,
Juliane was inside an airliner.
The next,
she was outside.
Alone in the sky.
Still strapped into her row of three seats.
Her mother was no longer beside her.
Years later,
she would put it in one sentence.
I hadn't left the plane.
The plane had left me.
She remembered the silence first.
The screaming had stopped.
Only the wind remained.
The row of seats was spinning.
And beneath her,
the forest was rushing up.
Then everything went black.
When she opened her eyes,
her watch said nine o'clock.
It was Christmas morning.
She was lying on the forest floor,
under her row of seats,
in the rain.
She had fallen about three kilometers.
Two miles.
And she was alive.
No one knows exactly why.
The row of seats may have spun like the blades of
a helicopter and slowed her fall.
The storm may have pushed her upward for a few seconds.
The canopy,
layer after layer of branches and vines,
may have caught her before the ground did.
Probably it was all of those things at once.
And a kind of luck that no physics can fully explain.
Her collarbone was broken.
So were the ligaments in one knee.
She had a deep,
open wound on her arm,
and a concussion.
One eye was swollen shut.
The other was barely a slit,
and both were red with burst blood vessels.
She had lost her glasses.
She was very short-sighted.
She was wearing a sleeveless minidress she had
bought with her savings for the graduation.
And only one sandal.
She called for her mother.
Again and again.
Nobody answered.
All around her,
the jungle went on as if nothing had happened.
Cicadas.
Frogs.
Birds.
The rain dripping from a hundred million leaves.
She would later say that what she felt was not fear.
It was a boundless feeling of abandonment.
She searched the area around her.
There was no wreckage.
No bodies.
No one.
Only a small bag of sweets,
lying in the mud.
It would be her only food.
She was alone in one of the largest rainforests on Earth.
And the clock had already started.
Then she heard something she recognised.
The sound of trickling water.
She found a tiny stream.
Barely a thread.
And she remembered her father's words.
Find moving water.
Never let it out of your sight.
So she began to walk.
Not through the forest,
but through the water itself.
In the stream,
she could see where she was going.
On either side,
the jungle was a wall.
Every step was dangerous.
Without her glasses,
the world was a blur.
She held her one sandal in front of her,
tapping the ground ahead,
testing every step.
In the rivers of the Amazon,
stingrays lie buried in the sand.
Snakes rest in the shallows.
Her parents had taught her to read all of it.
Above her,
she heard engines.
Search planes.
Helicopters.
She waved.
She shouted.
But from the air,
the canopy is a solid green roof.
A person standing beneath it simply does not exist.
After a few days,
the engines stopped coming.
She understood what that meant.
Within days,
the bag of sweets was empty.
On the fourth day,
she heard a sound that frightened her more than
any animal.
The call of king vultures.
Huge birds,
with naked,
painted heads.
They only come down to the ground in numbers when
something there is dead.
She knew exactly what that meant.
She followed them.
In a clearing,
she found a row of three seats,
driven head-first into the earth.
Three passengers were still strapped in.
A woman,
and two men.
They had been dead for days.
She did not want to look.
But she had to know.
With a stick,
she carefully touched the woman's foot.
The toenails were painted.
In her own words:
my mother never used polish on her nails.
It was not her.
She walked away,
and kept following the water.
The stream grew wider.
It became a brook.
Then a small river.
Now it was too deep to walk.
So she waded,
and when the current was gentle,
she swam.
She kept to the middle of the river.
Caimans rest along the banks.
In the open water,
they were less likely to come for her.
Around her,
she heard howler monkeys.
Hoatzins called from the branches over the water.
The real danger was smaller.
And it was already inside her.
The open wound on her arm had become infected.
Flies had laid their eggs in it.
The eggs had hatched.
Maggots were living in her arm.
Every afternoon,
the rain came.
Every night,
she lay on the riverbank,
shivering,
in a thin wet dress,
while insects covered her body.
She had nothing left to eat.
She drank the brown river water and kept moving.
She never truly panicked.
She simply kept walking.
Because there was nothing else to do.
Day after day,
her body burned through its last reserves.
She was starting to believe she would die alone
in the forest.
Then,
on the tenth day,
she saw something on the riverbank that did not
belong to the jungle.
A boat.
At first,
she thought she was hallucinating.
Next to it,
a path led up from the river.
And at the end of the path,
a small shelter.
People had been here.
Inside,
she found the fuel for the boat's motor.
And she remembered something her father had once
done for their dog,
when its wound filled with worms.
She poured the fuel over her arm.
The pain was enormous.
The maggots,
desperate for air,
began crawling out of the wound.
She pulled them out,
one by one.
Dozens of them.
She thought about taking the boat.
It could have carried her downriver.
But she could not bring herself to steal it.
So she stayed in the shelter,
lay down on the ground,
and waited.
She did not know if anyone would ever come back.
The next day,
she heard voices.
Men's voices.
Speaking Spanish.
She would later say it was like hearing the
voices of angels.
Three local lumbermen came walking up from the river.
This was their camp.
They saw a pale,
filthy girl lying in their shelter,
covered in bites and cuts,
her eyes blood-red.
At first,
they were afraid of her.
They thought she might be a water spirit.
A creature from the river.
Juliane spoke to them in Spanish.
She told them who she was.
That she had been on the plane that fell from the sky.
They had heard about it.
Everyone had.
They cleaned her wounds.
They gave her something to eat.
The next day,
they put her in a canoe and took her down the river.
The journey took about seven hours.
From there,
a missionary pilot flew her to Yarinacocha,
beside Pucallpa.
It was January the fourth,
1972.
Eleven days after the plane came apart in the sky.
Soon after,
her father reached her.
They held each other,
and for a long moment,
neither of them could speak.
Juliane then did something very few people would
have the strength to do.
She helped the search.
The planes had never found the wreckage.
Her memory did.
With the information she gave,
the teams finally reached the crash site.
The remains of the Electra were scattered across
several kilometers of forest.
On January the twelfth,
they found her mother's body.
And then came the hardest truth of all.
Juliane had not been the only one to survive the fall.
As many as fourteen people lived through the impact.
They died in the days that followed,
waiting for a rescue that never reached them.
Her mother may have been one of them.
Juliane had not waited.
She had walked.
Ninety-one people died on LANSA Flight 508.
On the day she was found,
the government cancelled the airline's permit.
It never flew again.
The world wanted her story.
Newspapers called her the girl who fell from the sky.
She was seventeen,
and grieving,
and suddenly famous.
She left Peru for Germany.
She did not go back for about fourteen years.
One question would follow her for the rest of her life.
Why was I the only survivor?
In 1998,
a German filmmaker came looking for her.
Werner Herzog.
He had his own strange link to the story.
In December 1971,
he was in Peru,
scouting locations for a film.
He very nearly took that same flight.
A last-minute change of plans saved him.
He took Juliane back to the jungle,
back to the place where she fell.
The film was called Wings of Hope.
She walked through the forest to the remains of
the Electra,
still lying among the trees.
Juliane did not run away from the jungle.
She went back to it.
She studied biology in Kiel,
the same city where her parents had met.
She earned a doctorate in Munich,
writing about bats.
She married an entomologist,
Erich Diller,
and became Juliane Diller.
And after her father died in the year 2000,
she took over Panguana.
At Panguana,
she has recorded more than fifty species of bats.
Almost twice as many as in the whole of Europe.
In 2011,
she published her memoir.
When I Fell From the Sky.
That same year,
Peru declared Panguana a private conservation area.
It began with less than two hundred hectares.
Today it protects about two and a half thousand.
The forest that saved her is the forest she now protects.
In 2019,
Peru awarded her one of its highest honours.
She has said that,
alone in the jungle,
she made a promise.
If she survived,
she would devote her life to something that
served nature and humanity.
She kept it.
Here is what makes this story so remarkable.
Juliane Koepcke was not strong.
She was not trained.
She had no equipment.
She was a seventeen-year-old girl in a summer dress,
with a broken collarbone and one shoe.
What she had was knowledge.
She knew the jungle was not an enemy.
It was a place with rules.
In her words,
it's not the green hell that the world always thinks.
She knew which dangers were real,
and which were only frightening.
She knew that water leads to people.
And she knew that nobody was coming.
So she went to them.
For days,
the search planes flew over her head.
Every one of them missed her.
In the end,
there was no rescue.
There was only a girl,
following the water.
If this story stayed with you,
subscribe to No Rescue.
Every week,
we tell another true story of someone who
survived when no one was coming.
Thank you for watching.
